Existing methods are often limited by their underlying physical models, making it challenging to achieve single-shot, non-invasive multispectral imaging through scattering media. In this Letter, a speckle correlation model for the single-shot imaging of multispectral targets is developed. By using a gradient descent method based on differentiable computation, efficient multispectral imaging through scattering media is achieved. The method requires no additional system modulation and uses only minimal computational resources for fast reconstruction. Reconstruction results obtained by conventional methods and by the proposed method are compared under increasing spectral differences. Additionally, the proposed method can image hidden targets with spectral differences of up to 160 nm.

In this Letter, a physical model for multispectral target imaging through a scattering medium is proposed. Based on differentiable computing, this model enables imaging of multiple multispectral targets behind a scattering medium using a single frame of speckle. Such single-shot multispectral imaging capability is important for practical scenarios in which different object components possess distinct spectral responses but are spatially mixed by scattering. Representative examples include multi-stained biological samples, spectrally labeled targets, and multispectral coded structures hidden behind turbid or diffusive media. When light propagates forward through a scattering medium of thickness L, the medium can be discretized into multiple layers of random phase plates. The light field at zp after passing through the pth layer of random phase plates can be expressed as
Ek(p)(r⊥,zp)=∫Ẽk(p)(θp) exp[ik(r⊥·θp+zp(1−θp22))]d2θp,
(1)
where r⊥=(x,y) represents the coordinates in the plane orthogonal to the optical axis, θp is the small deflection angle of the plane wave relative to the optical axis, which is a two-dimensional vector defined in the X and Y directions, respectively, and Ẽk(p)(θp) is the angular spectrum amplitude.27,28
The cross correlation function of two light beams with different wavelengths after passing through the scattering medium is defined as
C(k,k′;z,z′)=⟨Ek(r⊥,z)Ek′*(r⊥,z′)⟩,
(2)
where k and k′ are the wavevectors corresponding to the two wavelengths. By considering the statistical properties of the scattering process and performing integration, the following expression is obtained:
C=11+(k0LΘ02)218+(Θ02k′(k(z′+L/3)−k′(z+L/3)))2,
(3)
where k0=k−k′k′⁠. The condition for the extremum is given by
(Θ02k′(k(z′+L/3)−k′(z+L/3)))2=0,
(4)
which indicates that the correlation between the scattering signals of the two wavelengths is maximized, and
k(z′+L/3)=k′(z+L/3)⇒λλ′=z′+L/3z+L/3,
(5)
which means when the incident wavelength undergoes a slight change, the axial position of the corresponding effective detection plane shifts. As a result, the correlation of speckle patterns for different wavelengths decreases, a phenomenon referred to as the chromatic axial memory effect.27,28 Detailed derivations are provided in the supplementary material.

The constraint logic is illustrated in Fig. 2, and the complete algorithmic structure is presented in Algorithm 1. The entire iterative process is performed using PyTorch to execute the standard automatic differentiation gradient descent optimization. Since this method only uses gradient descent for constraint iterations, the algorithm has relatively low time and space complexity. The time complexity is O(num_iters×H×Wlog(H×W))⁠, and the space complexity is O(H×W)⁠, where num_iters represents the number of iterations, and H and W denote the height and width of the image, respectively. All computations are performed on a CPU (Intel i9 9700K) and a GPU (Nvidia RTX TITAN). When the input image size is 256 × 256, the GPU memory usage is only 1.3 GB.

Algorithm 1.

Reconstruction of multispectral targets from speckle autocorrelation.

1: Input: Speckle autocorrelation C⁠, Number of iterations num_iters⁠, Learning rate lr, Regularization weights (λTV,λC,λS,λL1)
2: Output: Reconstructed targets r1,r2…rn
3: System Initialization:
  • Compute Power Spectral Density of input autocorrelation:
          PC=|FFT(C)|
  • Initialize r1,r2…rn randomly
4: for iter=1 to num_iters do
5:  Zero gradients for each ri⁠:
          ∇ri=0
6: Step 1: Compute Autocorrelation and Power Spectrum Density:
         Ci=corr(ri)
        PCi=|FFT(Ci)|
7: Step 2: Total Loss Calculation:
  Loss=λTV·∑nLossTV(ri)+λC·∑nLossC(ri)+λS·∑nLossS(ri)+λL 1·LossL1(∑nPCi/n,PC)
8: Step 3: Update with Optimizer:
  • Perform gradient backpropagation and update ri via Adam optimizer:
       ri(t+1)=Adam(ri(t),∇riLoss,lr)
9: Step 4: Adaptive Learning Rate Update:
  • Update learning rate based on current loss using Reduce LR On Plateau scheduler:
          scheduler.step(Loss)
10: end for
11: Output: Final reconstructed targets ri
